title: What should you do in the 30 minutes before a case interview?
description: A calm 30-minute routine for the half hour before your interview: familiar reading, a speech warm-up, one short mock and time to settle.
hook: In the 30 minutes before a case interview, warm up skills you already have: ten minutes of familiar reading, five minutes of speech warm-up, ten minutes of one short, easy mock, and five minutes to settle. Do not learn anything new or attempt a full hard case. The aim is to arrive rested, warm and able to think flexibly, not tired and full of half-remembered lists.
body:
The 30-minute plan

  1. 10 minutes: familiar reading. Skim your own vocabulary notes, a business book you have already read, or the summary of a framework you know well. Look for ideas you already understand, not new jargon.
  2. 5 minutes: speech warm-up. Read one paragraph aloud at a calm pace, or follow a short guided routine such as Speech On (speechon.app, free). Loosen your jaw and practise clear articulation, especially on numbers.
  3. 10 minutes: one short mock. Recap a simple prompt, outline three branches, do two straightforward percentage calculations and give a 30 to 60 second answer-first recommendation. Then stop. Focus on one thing only, such as leading with the answer.
  4. 5 minutes: settle. Check your materials, have water nearby, breathe slowly for a minute or two (breathing out for longer than you breathe in helps many people) and remind yourself the interviewer wants you to do well.

Sort the practical details the day before

Last-minute uncertainty uses up attention you need for the case. The day before, check:

  • the location and travel time, or the video link, software and a quiet room;
  • the time zone, if the interviewer is in another country;
  • plain paper, two pens and a calculator only if you have been told it is allowed;
  • your stories and your "Why this firm?" notes, so you only need to glance at them on the day.

A technical problem is not a test of business ability, but it can rattle you if it is a surprise. Join video calls a few minutes early.

What not to do

  • Do not learn a new framework. It will crowd out the structures you know and you will be tempted to force it in.
  • Do not do a full, hard case. If it goes badly, you walk in shaken. If it goes well, you are tired.
  • Do not build a rigid ritual. If the plan slips because a train is late, that is fine. The interview does not depend on a particular exercise.

Being rested matters more than one extra hour of practice. Sleep the night before beats late-night cramming every time.

If the warm-up goes wrong

If you make a small arithmetic slip in your mini-mock, correct it calmly and move on. Do not launch into a remedial session. A mistake 20 minutes before the interview is useful: it reminds you to slow down on numbers. It is not a forecast.

Try it: a 10-minute mini-mock

Use this as your warm-up case. Say everything out loud.

A chain of bike shops has seen profit fall from $2M to $1.5M in a year. The owner wants to know why.
Show a strong answer

Recap: "Profit fell by $0.5M, which is 25%, and we want to find out why."

Three branches: revenue (number of bikes and services sold, average price), costs (variable costs such as stock and staff hours, fixed costs such as rent) and anything one-off or outside the business, such as a new competitor nearby.

Quick sum: if costs rose by $300k, that explains $300k ÷ $500k = 60% of the fall, leaving $200k to find in revenue.

Recommendation, answer first: "Most of the profit fall comes from higher costs, so I'd start by breaking down which cost lines grew, then check whether sales volumes also slipped."

Where to go next

If nerves are the real issue, read how to stay calm when nerves hit. If the interview is a few days away, follow the one-week plan. For a quick maths warm-up, two minutes of the case maths drill is ideal, and the 60-second recommendation shows how to close.
